overview.body:
**Mnw** ​(*min*) — ‌Fertility, the ‌Eastern ​Desert, Male ​Potency · ​The ​firm one ​— belongs ‌to ​the Egyptian ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Fertility, ‌Harvest". ​The name ​means "The ​firm ​one"[^1].

**Mnw** ​— Min ‌— ​is the ‌lightning-rod god ​of ‌male fertility: ​erect, flail ‌raised, ​lettuce-crowned, lord ‌of the ​desert ​roads to ‌the Red ‌Sea and ‌of ​everything that ​stands firm. ‌The ​Greeks saw ​Pan in ‌him; ​the Egyptians ​saw the ‌power ​that makes ‌the land ​and ​its people ​endure — ​*mn*, ‌the root ‌of his ​name, ‌means ‘to ​remain’.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ‌as **Mnw** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/min/). ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a ​description computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *min* ‌survives as ​a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the ​name ​is ​**/mɪn/ (conventional)** ​— ‌Conventional ​reading ​— ‌Egyptian ​vocalisation ‌not ​attested.[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ​**Mnw** ​— ​Written ‌mnw; conventionally ​vocalised ‌“Min”. ​The ‌name ​relates ‌to ​mn, ‌“to ​be ​firm, ‌enduring”.
- ‌**** ‌— ​Two ​consonants, one ‌certain ​vowel: ​the ‌oldest ​god ​of ‌the ​eastern ‌desert.

​For ​the ​modern ​speaker, ‌the closest ‌approximation ​is: ‌“MIN”

​Kindred ​and ‌historical ‌forms ‌of ‌the ​name:

- ‌**Greek** ​— ​Πᾶν ​(Pan) ‌in Herodotus’ ​equation

​Herodotus ​(2.46) ‌says ​the ​Egyptians ​“are ‌the ​only ‌people ​who ‌have ​a ‌Pan” ‌— Min. ​The ​name ​crossed ​into ‌Greek ‌without ​respelling.

sources.citation: Herodotus, Histories 2.46 (the procession and the Pan-equation).
James P. Allen, Middle Egyptian: An Introduction to the Language and Culture of Hieroglyphs, Cambridge University Press, 2000.
Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian.

domains.body:
**Mnw** ​— Min ‌— is ‌the ​lightning-rod god ​of ​male fertility: ​erect, flail ​raised, ‌lettuce-crowned, lord ​of ​the desert ‌roads to ​the ‌Red Sea ​and of ‌everything ​that stands ​firm. ​The Greeks ​saw Pan ​in ‌him; the ​Egyptians ‌saw the ​power that ‌makes ​the land ‌and ​its people ‌endure — ​*mn*, ​the root ‌of his ‌name, ‌means ‘to ​remain’.[^1]

### ​The Firm ‌One

His ​name ​is the ‌verb ​“to be ​enduring”; he ‌is ​the god ‌of what ​stands ​fast — ​harvests, ​dynasties, erections.

### ‌Lord of ‌the ​Desert Roads

‌Master ​of the ​eastern highlands ‌and ‌the routes ‌to the ‌Red ​Sea gold ‌mines.

### ​Fertility in ​the Fields

​The ‌lettuce — ​an ​aphrodisiac to ​the Egyptians ‌— ​and the ​flail ​of the ‌harvest belong ​to ‌his iconography.

### ​The Processional ‌God

​His festival ‌raised ‌his image ​on its ​litter ​in public ​procession ‌— Egypt’s ‌most ancient ​god-ritual.

sources.citation: Festival reliefs of the Ramesseum and Medinet Habu (the Min procession).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Mnw ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- **The ​Firm ​One** ​— ​His ​name is ‌the ​verb ‌“to ​be enduring”; ‌he ​is ‌the ​god ‌of what ​stands ​fast ‌— ‌harvests, ‌dynasties, erections.
- ​**Lord ​of ‌the ​Desert Roads** ​— ‌Master ​of ​the ‌eastern highlands ​and ‌the ​routes ​to ​the Red ​Sea ‌gold ‌mines.
- ​**Fertility in ‌the ​Fields** ​— ‌The ‌lettuce — ‌an ‌aphrodisiac ​to ‌the ​Egyptians — ​and ​the ‌flail ​of the ​harvest ​belong ‌to ​his ​iconography.
- **The ​Processional ‌God** ​— ‌His festival ​raised ‌his ​image ‌on ‌its litter ​in ​public ​procession ​— ‌Egypt’s most ‌ancient ​god-ritual.

sources.citation: Herodotus, Histories 2.46 (the procession and the Pan-equation).

mythology.body:
Min has ​no narrative myth-cycle; his ‌‘stories’ are the ‌rituals that stage ​him — the processions, ​the erect phallus, ​the lettuce beds of ​his gardens — ​and the oldest ‌continuous cult record of ​any Egyptian god. ​His mythology is written ‌in the calendar: ​his great festival closed ‌the harvest and ​opened the desert’s ‌travelling season.[^1]

### Older Than ​the Kings (Predynastic ​Origins)

Min’s emblem appears ​on the artefacts ​of the late ​Predynastic — the famous ‌Min-standard carved on ​the maceheads of King ‌Scorpion and Narmer’s ​age. Before Horus ‌belonged to the king, ​Min belonged to ‌the land: the lightning-rod, ​the ithyphallic pillar, ‌the force that ​stood behind fertility itself.[^2]

### ​The Procession at ‌the Harvest (Festival of ‌Min)

His great ‌festival in the month ​of Shemu opened ​with the king ‌cutting a sheaf of ​emmer — the ​‘coming forth of Min’ ‌from his shrine ​on the shoulders ​of his priests, carried ‌to the acclaim ​of the crowd, followed ‌by the ritual ​release of four ​wild birds to the ​four winds. The ​rite married the harvest ‌to virility: the ‌cut grain and ​the standing god are ‌one mystery.

### The ​Only People with a ​Pan (Herodotus)

Herodotus ‌describes Min’s procession at ‌Chemmis — the ‌carrying shrine, the ‌phallic imagery — and ​concludes that the ‌Egyptian Min is the ​original of the ​Greek Pan, the ​same god under two ‌names. It is ​the earliest comparative-religion argument ​in Western literature, ​and it was ‌made about Min.

### Husband ​of Repyt and ​Isis (Divine Consort)

At ​Coptos he was ‌paired with the ​lioness-goddess Repyt, ‘the Weary ‌One’ who nonetheless ​endures; in the wider ‌Osirian orbit his ​fertility stands behind Horus’ ‌conception. In the ‌Late Period his ​statue was carried to ​the graveyards to ​visit Osiris — the ​fertility god paying ‌his respects to ‌the dead one, generation ​greeting dissolution.

hieroglyphic-evidence.body:
The name Mnw is written in Egyptian hieroglyphs as a theonym with the divine determinative. Scribes used logographic and phonetic signs to represent the sounds and semantic class of the deity.

The restoration Mnw transliterates Egyptological convention, preserving the distinction between sign function and phonetic value.[^1]

sources.citation: Herodotus, Histories 2.46 (the procession and the Pan-equation).

pyramid-texts.body:
The Pyramid Texts, inscribed in royal tombs of the Old Kingdom, contain the earliest references to Mnw. These spells map the king's journey through the afterlife and the divine forces that assist or oppose him.

The restored name Mnw reflects scholarly transliteration of those hieroglyphic spells.[^1]

sources.citation: Herodotus, Histories 2.46 (the procession and the Pan-equation).

coffin-texts.body:
The Coffin Texts democratize the afterlife knowledge of the Pyramid Texts, inscribing spells on private coffins of the Middle Kingdom. Mnw appears in mortuary and cosmological passages that protect the deceased.

The Unicode restoration Mnw continues the Egyptological reading of those texts.[^1]

sources.citation: Herodotus, Histories 2.46 (the procession and the Pan-equation).

book-of-the-dead.body:
The Book of the Dead, a New Kingdom compilation of spells, includes references and imagery connected with Mnw. Papyri and tomb vignettes present the deity in the landscape of judgment and transformation.

The restored spelling Mnw preserves the scholarly form used in modern editions.[^1]

sources.citation: Herodotus, Histories 2.46 (the procession and the Pan-equation).
